ENCOUNTER NOTE
Date: 2022-01-15
Provider: Dr. David Park, MD
Department: Pediatric Endocrinology
Visit Type: outpatient

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Several weeks of increasing fatigue, reduced energy, headaches, and difficulty seeing the classroom chalkboard.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient returns to Pediatric Endocrinology, previously seen in this department in July 2020 for Gaucher disease. He has recently developed difficulty reading the chalkboard from his seat and occasionally bumps into objects on his left side. His appetite has also declined, and his parents have noticed that his shoes and clothes still fit him the same despite his classmates outgrowing theirs.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
Active Problem List:
- X-linked Hyper-IgM Syndrome (CD40 Ligand Deficiency) (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Gaucher disease (diagnosed 2020-07-15)
- Vesicoureteral reflux with recurrent UTI (diagnosed 2021-01-15)
- Ureteropelvic junction obstruction (diagnosed 2021-07-15)
- Cystic fibrosis with pancreatic insufficiency
- Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
- Craniopharyngioma
- HIV infection
- Vesicoureteral reflux
- Nutritional rickets secondary to malabsorption

PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:
- Central venous catheter placement
- Subtotal resection of craniopharyngioma

MEDICATIONS:
Home Medications:
- Pancrelipase 3 capsules with meals and snacks
- Imiglucerase 60 units/kg IV every 2 weeks
- Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 5 mg/kg TMP PO daily (PCP prophylaxis)
- Vitamin D3 2000 IU PO daily
- Calcium carbonate 500 mg PO twice daily
- Antiretroviral therapy Age-appropriate combination therapy per pediatric HIV protocol
- Maintenance chemotherapy for ALL Per current oncology protocol

ALLERGIES:
No known drug allergies (NKDA)

FAMILY HISTORY:
- Mother is a carrier for X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome
- Both parents are carriers for cystic fibrosis and Gaucher disease
- Paternal history of HIV infection

SOCIAL HISTORY:
Smoking: Never. Alcohol: Never. Occupation: Elementary school student.

VITAL SIGNS:
His temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 84/min, and blood pressure is 106/70 mmHg.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
Visual field testing reveals decreased peripheral vision bilaterally.

LABORATORY DATA:
Hormonal evaluation shows reduced serum IGF-1 and borderline low cortisol.

IMAGING:
A non-contrast MRI of the brain reveals a suprasellar, partially calcified mass compressing the optic chiasm.

ENCOUNTER NOTE
Date: 2023-01-15
Provider: Dr. David Park, MD
Department: Pediatric Endocrinology
Visit Type: outpatient

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Chronic fatigue, difficulty walking, and frequent bone pain over the past 6 months despite pancreatic enzyme replacement.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient is a 10-year-old male with cystic fibrosis with pancreatic insufficiency, previously evaluated in this department for Gaucher disease and craniopharyngioma, who returns for assessment of persistent malabsorptive and musculoskeletal symptoms. His mother reports that he continues to have frequent bulky, foul-smelling stools that float in the toilet bowl, despite adherence to pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy. She notes that his stools are difficult to flush and often leave an oily film in the water. Over the past 6 months, he has been complaining of aching in his legs, especially after running, and difficulty climbing stairs. She has also noticed that he seems to tire more easily than other children his age and prefers sedentary activities such as drawing instead of outdoor play.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
Active Problem List:
- X-linked Hyper-IgM Syndrome (CD40 Ligand Deficiency) (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Gaucher disease (diagnosed 2020-07-15)
- Vesicoureteral reflux with recurrent UTI (diagnosed 2021-01-15)
- Ureteropelvic junction obstruction (diagnosed 2021-07-15)
- Craniopharyngioma (diagnosed 2022-01-15)
- HIV infection (diagnosed 2022-07-15)
- Cystic fibrosis with pancreatic insufficiency
- Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
- Vesicoureteral reflux
- Nutritional rickets secondary to malabsorption

The child was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 2 after recurrent respiratory infections and failure to thrive prompted genetic testing, which confirmed a mutation in the CFTR gene. Since that time, he has required repeated hospitalizations for pneumonia, most commonly with Pseudomonas aeruginosa , and is on a regimen of inhaled antibiotics, bronchodilators, and chest physiotherapy.

PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:
- Central venous catheter placement
- Subtotal resection of craniopharyngioma

MEDICATIONS:
Home Medications:
- Pancrelipase 3 capsules with meals and snacks
- Imiglucerase 60 units/kg IV every 2 weeks
- Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 5 mg/kg TMP PO daily (PCP prophylaxis)
- Vitamin D3 2000 IU PO daily
- Calcium carbonate 500 mg PO twice daily
- Antiretroviral therapy Age-appropriate combination therapy per pediatric HIV protocol
- Maintenance chemotherapy for ALL Per current oncology protocol

ALLERGIES:
No known drug allergies (NKDA)

FAMILY HISTORY:
His family history is significant for an older sibling who also has cystic fibrosis and required a lung transplant at age 15. His parents are non-consanguineous and healthy.

SOCIAL HISTORY:
The child lives in a suburban home with his family and attends school regularly, but has missed several days due to illness.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS:
On review of systems, the mother adds that he has had poor appetite, irritability, and occasional abdominal bloating. She denies recent trauma but is concerned that he may have nutritional deficiencies. He has not had any seizures or syncope.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
On examination, his height is at the 5th percentile and weight at the 3rd percentile for age. He appears thin with minimal subcutaneous fat. His sclerae are anicteric, but there is generalized pallor. The chest shows mild pectus excavatum with scattered crackles bilaterally on auscultation. Cardiac examination is normal. The abdomen is soft but mildly distended. His extremities are thin, and he walks with a slightly waddling gait. There is tenderness to palpation over the shins and femurs. Neurologic examination reveals normal cranial nerves, intact sensation, but mild proximal muscle weakness. Deep tendon reflexes are present and symmetric.

LABORATORY DATA:
Laboratory evaluation reveals hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and elevated alkaline phosphatase. 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels are markedly reduced.

IMAGING:
A DEXA scan shows decreased bone mineral density consistent with rickets/osteomalacia.
